attribution.note: Marcus's own words in his own Substack post, endorsed. He is not quoting anyone; he is rebutting Vance's remarks.

semantics.note: Keeps both parts and marks 'arguably' as a hedge on the 'almost none' part. That part is graded confidence and is not scored. Only the firm claim that Vance lacks any evidence is scoreable, and it reads close to rhetoric.

contract.note: The ordinary reading of 'AI regulation', taken to include sectoral and state rules, is fair. But the support condition also asks for regulation to be 'exceptionally limited', which scores the hedged 'arguably' part; under policy that part should not count. Whether Vance had evidence depends on what he possessed, not on what he cited, so the result turns on interpretation.

evidence.note: The full speech gives EU examples (GDPR, DSA) rather than US-specific ones. That shows he cited no US evidence, but not that he possessed none.

A 2024 FCC ruling applying robocall rules to AI voices was in force on the target date. It is one targeted rule, consistent with 'almost' none, and that part is hedged anyway. It says nothing about Vance's evidence.
A June 2025 CRS report: no broad federal AI law, but targeted provisions and state laws exist. It is a later snapshot, so context only, and it does not address the burden or Vance's evidence.

reviews.rationale: The 'almost none' part is hedged ('arguably') and is not scored. The firm part, that Vance had no evidence whatsoever of excessive US AI regulation, is not settled by the packet. The speech cites only EU rules, which shows nothing about what evidence Vance held. Nothing in the packet assesses US regulatory burden. FCC and CRS items show targeted rules existed, but they bear on the hedged part. The packet's own stated gaps confirm the record is incomplete.
